findings.headline: Multiple major capital schemes show deferrals of 50% or more, including Toutley depot (56%), ASC accommodation transformation (73%), and MEES investment (52%)
findings.detail: In addition to Grays Farm, several other significant capital projects show substantial deferrals: Toutley depot refurbishment (£2.6m of £4.6m), ASC accommodation transformation (£2.0m of £2.7m), and MEES energy investment (£3.2m of £6.2m). These deferrals span Place & Growth, Adult Social Care, and Resources & Assets.
findings.matters: Multiple major capital schemes being deferred at rates above 50% suggests potential systemic constraints in capital delivery, whether in planning, procurement, funding, or execution across multiple service areas
findings.figures: Toutley: £4.6m budget, £2.6m deferred (56%); ASC accommodation: £2.7m budget, £2.0m deferred (73%); MEES: £6.2m budget, £3.2m deferred (52%)
findings.quote: Toutley depot refurbishment 4,566,903 0 2,566,903 2,566,903; ASC accommodation transformation 2,727,624 0 2,000,000 2,000,000; MEES Investment 6,248,173 0 3,248,173 3,248,173

findings.headline: Grays Farm sports hub has £5.3 million (84%) of its £6.3 million current-year budget deferred, the most heavily slipped project
findings.detail: The Grays Farm sports hub project has an approved current-year budget of £6.25 million with £5.25 million newly identified for carry forward. This represents one of the highest deferral rates in the capital programme.
findings.matters: Significant deferral of a major service infrastructure project suggests material delays in design, procurement, or planning that warrant investigation and may impact when intended service benefits are realised
findings.figures: Approved budget: £6.25m; Carry forward: £5.25m (84% deferred)

findings.headline: £19.2 million (36.5% of the current-year £52.7 million approved capital budget) is being carried forward to future years
findings.detail: As of end of June 2026, the council has identified a total carry forward of £19.2 million of newly deferred capital across its programme. This includes deferrals in Adult Social Care & Health (£4.0m), Housing Revenue Account (£0.2m), Place & Growth (£8.6m), and Resources & Assets (£6.0m). All of these deferrals are newly identified in the quarter with no previously agreed carry forwards being adjusted.
findings.matters: Material mid-year capital programme slippage of over one-third of approved spend affects future budget pressures and raises questions about the council's ability to deliver capital projects within planned timescales
findings.figures: Total approved budget: £52.7m; Total carry forward: £19.2m (36.5%)
findings.quote: Total reprofiling identified as at end of June 2026 52,674,727 0 19,243,169 19,243,169

findings.headline: Place & Growth overspend of £550k with undelivered savings and waste contract risk
findings.detail: Place & Growth is forecasting £550k overspend due to enforcement staffing, bus pass demand, undeliverable grounds maintenance savings (grass cutting), and delayed on-street parking implementation. Waste disposal contract risks remain unresolved despite external support being brought in.
findings.matters: Multiple undelivered savings and unresolved contract risks indicate implementation challenges and suggest budget planning assumptions are not being met.
findings.figures: Place & Growth: Budget £47,493k; Forecast £48,043k; Overspend £550k
findings.quote: undeliverable grounds maintenance saving involving grass cutting and delays to the implementation of on street parking charges. Further risks exist mainly in relation to the waste disposal contract

findings.headline: Children's Services overspending by £1m due to increasing complexity and cost of placements
findings.detail: Children's Services is forecast to overspend by £990k. The council notes the number of children in care is stable relative to population, but the cost per child is rising significantly, with some individual placements costing more than double the budgeted amount.
findings.matters: Unpredictable and uncontrollable unit cost increases for vulnerable children represent a structural budget risk that cannot be easily managed through operational efficiency.
findings.figures: Children's Services: Budget £56,095k; Forecast £57,085k; Overspend £990k
findings.quote: the complexity and cost of placing these children continues to increase with a few cases costing more than double the average budgeted

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspending by £1.5m due to population growth and increasing complexity
findings.detail: The largest single overspend is Adult Social Care at £1.512m. The council attributes this to continuing population growth and increasing complexity, explicitly stating this represents 'a more significant rise than seen in previous years, building on the pressures experienced in 2025/26'.
findings.matters: Growing demand and unit costs in adult social care without corresponding budget increases represent a structural pressure likely to recur, indicating unsustainable budget assumptions.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care: Budget £85,855k; Forecast £87,367k; Overspend £1,512k
findings.quote: Population growth and complexity are expected to continue increasing, representing a more significant rise than seen in previous years, building on the pressures experienced in 2025/26 and now resulting in a predicted overspend of £1.5m.

findings.headline: General fund forecasted to overspend by £3.3m mid-year
findings.detail: The council's approved general fund budget of £210.2m is forecast to reach £213.5m outturn, a net overspend of £3.3m. This material variance is recorded at the halfway point of the financial year.
findings.matters: A £3.3m overspend indicates the council cannot live within its budget and will require either spending cuts or reserve drawdown to balance the year, both significant concerns for lenders.
findings.figures: Current Approved Budget £210,235k; Forecast Outturn £213,527k; Net overspend £3,292k
findings.quote: Net Expenditure 210,235 213,527 3,292

findings.headline: Children's services case complexity driving cost increases despite stable placement numbers
findings.detail: Children's Services is forecasting a £990k overspend. The council notes that whilst the number of children in care is stable relative to the growing population, the complexity and cost of placements continues to rise, with 'a few cases costing more than double the average budgeted'. UASC pressures are being met from one-off grants and reserves but are expected to become a growth pressure.
findings.matters: The council faces structural cost inflation in children's placements as case complexity increases; this is a structural pressure unlikely to resolve without service model change, and UASC costs moving from one-off to recurring pressures.
findings.figures: £990k overspend forecast
findings.quote: Whilst the number of children in care is relatively stable as a proportion of our growing population, the complexity and cost of placing these children continues to increase with a few cases costing more than double the average budgeted

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £1.5m driven by population growth and case complexity
findings.detail: Adult Social Care is forecasting a £1.512m overspend. The council reports that population growth and complexity are increasing faster than in previous years, 'building on the pressures experienced in 2025/26'. The council states 'careful governance and robust financial management will remain essential priorities' to manage these pressures.
findings.matters: Adult social care demand pressures are typically difficult to control; if growth and complexity are accelerating faster than budgeted, this service may face recurring overspends and impact the council's overall financial resilience.
findings.figures: £1.512m overspend
findings.quote: Population growth and complexity are expected to continue increasing, representing a more significant rise than seen in previous years, building on the pressures experienced in 2025/26 and now resulting in a predicted overspend of £1.5m

findings.headline: HRA reserve forecast to fall to £330k, below prudent 5% level of £1.08m
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is forecasting a £498k overspend in 2026/27 due to service improvement transition costs and temporary staffing. This will be covered from reserves, leaving the HRA reserve at approximately £330k by 31 March 2027, which is lower than the desired prudent level of £1.08m (5% of HRA expenditure budget).
findings.matters: HRA reserves falling below prudent levels reduces the council's resilience to unplanned maintenance costs or income volatility in housing; HRA is separately financed and impacts borrowing capacity for housing investment.
findings.figures: £498k overspend; forecast reserve balance £330k; prudent level 5% or £1.08m
findings.quote: The forecast £498k overspend will be covered from the HRA reserve. This forecast demand on the reserve along with the budgeted usage of the reserve in 2026/27 will result in the 31st March 2027 balance being c£330k. This is lower than desired level of reserves which is 5% of the expenditure budget (£1.08m)

findings.headline: Grounds maintenance saving of £250k already not deliverable
findings.detail: The council's approved 2026/27 budget included a £250k MTFP saving by reducing grass cutting from 4 to 2 cuts per year. Following contract negotiations, this saving is confirmed as undeliverable and will no longer be implemented. This represents a failure of the approved efficiency plan.
findings.matters: A key approved saving is already at risk in Q1; this signals weakness in the council's ability to deliver its £8m savings plan and suggests other savings may also face delivery risk.
findings.quote: Following contract negotiations with the grounds maintenance supplier this change is no longer considered deliverable. The recommendation is therefore that this saving is no longer implemented

findings.headline: Q1 overspend of £3.3m signals persistent service pressures across all directorates
findings.detail: Despite an £8m planned savings programme, the council is forecasting a £3.3m general fund overspend at Q1, with all directorates reporting pressures. Adult Social Care is £1.5m over, Children's Services £990k over. The council is 'working intensively' on the savings programme but early delivery is uncertain.
findings.matters: Early overspends in Q1 typically persist; if the council cannot deliver its £8m savings plan whilst covering existing overspends, end-of-year reserves will be drawn significantly, weakening liquidity.
findings.figures: £3.3m general fund overspend; £8 million planned savings and efficiencies; Adult Social Care £1.512m over; Children's Services £990k over
findings.quote: At quarter one, the Council is projecting an overspend of £3.3 million. Initial monitoring indicates financial pressures emerging across all Council services, with particularly notable pressures within Adult Social Care and Children's Services

findings.headline: DSG cumulative deficit of £73.3m with uncertain future grant support
findings.detail: The council faces a £20.4m in-year DSG deficit in 2026/27, driven by high needs block growth. Combined with the brought-forward £52.9m deficit, this reaches £73.3m cumulatively. Critically, the Safety Valve programme ended 31 March 2026, and replacement High Needs Stability Grant amounts are 'still unknown and yet to be determined' through 2028.
findings.matters: A £73m deficit in a hypothecated grant is a major structural problem for the council's overall finances and borrowing capacity; the uncertainty about future grant support makes medium-term forecasting unreliable.
findings.figures: £20.4m in-year deficit; £52.9m brought forward; £73.3m cumulative deficit as at 31 March 2027
findings.quote: An in-year deficit of £20.4m is forecast, with the budget pressure continuing to be felt within the High Needs Block. Taken with the brought forward deficit of £52.9m, a forecast cumulative deficit of £73.3m is now projected to the 31 March 2027

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review will cut council baseline funding by £20m per annum by 2028/29
findings.detail: Over three years, the council faces a £43m+ funding loss, with an ongoing £20m annual reduction by 2028/29. This is explicitly described as the most significant and adverse funding settlement the council has ever received. Officers are working on additional Medium Term Financial Planning options for 2027/28 onward.
findings.matters: This is an existential funding pressure that will require structural service reductions or significant council tax increases; lenders need to understand the council's capacity to service debt against a shrinking funding base.
findings.figures: £43 million over three years; £20 million per annum by 2028/29
findings.quote: Over the three-year implementation period, the Council is expected to lose in excess of £43 million of Government funding, resulting in an ongoing reduction in baseline funding of approximately £20 million per annum by 2028/29. This represents the most significant and adverse funding settlement the Council has ever received

findings.headline: Council commits to £1.57m capital loan for Loddon Homes affordable housing contingent on Homes England co-funding
findings.detail: The council approved a capital loan of up to £1,570,000 from existing approved capital loans budget to support an affordable housing scheme within Loddon Homes, plus £784,000 of S106 developer funding. The funding is conditional on the project securing Homes England funding. The council expects unquantified cost avoidance savings through specialist accommodation provision but no figure is given.
findings.matters: Material conditional commitment with execution risk—actual spend depends on Homes England approval, and failure to secure external funding could affect capital programme flexibility.
findings.figures: £1,570,000 capital loan; £784,000 S106 developer funding
findings.quote: The Council will also lend up to £1,570,000 as a capital loan, from the existing approved capital loans budget. Funding will be provided on the basis on the project securing Homes England funding in conjunction.

findings.headline: General fund balance in deficit: £6.8m at March 2027, improved from £10.1m deficit the previous year
findings.detail: The council's general fund balance is (£6,799)k at 31 March 2027, down from a deficit of (£10,091)k at 31 March 2026. The £3.3m improvement comes from service variances: Adult Social Care £1.5m, Children's Services £990k, Place & Growth £550k, Resources £140k, and Chief Executive £100k.
findings.matters: A persistent deficit general fund balance means the council is drawing down reserves rather than maintaining a positive buffer, signalling potential sustainability concerns if underlying budget pressures are not resolved
findings.quote: Estimated General Fund Balance (as at 31/3/2026) (£10,091); Estimated General Fund Balance 31/3/2027 (£6,799)

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management 202526 - Outturn - draft for CLT, 25/06/2026 Executive, 07/07/2026 Executive Briefing
findings.headline: Government DSG grant to support council deficits has been announced but details remain unknown
findings.detail: The government has announced grant funding to help local authorities fund DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) deficit balances, which the council expects to be 'positive' for cash flow and 'help manage future external borrowing need'. However, the council states 'Details of the grant payments are still to be understood', creating uncertainty over timing and quantum. The council's forward cash flow projections implicitly assume receipt of this grant.
findings.matters: Forward cash projections and borrowing forecasts depend on uncertain grant funding; delay or reduction in the announced grant could materially tighten cash flow and force earlier or larger external borrowing
findings.figures: No quantified figures; grant details to be announced
findings.quote: As part of the finance settlement, the government announced plans to provide grant funding to local authorities to help fund DSG deficit balances. Details of the grant payments are still to be understood.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management 202526 - Outturn - draft for CLT, 25/06/2026 Executive, 07/07/2026 Executive Briefing
findings.headline: Council is dependent on commercial and service investment income for approximately 10% of net revenue stream
findings.detail: Net income from commercial and service investments represents 9.25% of the council's net revenue stream. While the council characterizes this as 'relatively modest', this income stream is nevertheless material and depends on the performance of town centre regeneration, commercial property investments, and loans to housing companies. The council has explicitly noted 'risk' in its ambitious capital programme relating to housing, economy, and regeneration.
findings.matters: Material revenue funding depends on commercial asset performance; if these assets underperform, capital values fall, or housing companies struggle, the council's revenue budget and debt servicing capacity could face pressure; lender should understand concentration of this income
findings.figures: Commercial & service investment income = 9.25% of net revenue stream (improved from 8.87% forecast)
findings.quote: For Wokingham, although this is an important income stream to support the funding of vital services, the % is relatively modest at c10%.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management 202526 - Outturn - draft for CLT, 25/06/2026 Executive, 07/07/2026 Executive Briefing
findings.headline: Council is depleting cash reserves (£248m internal borrowing) to avoid external borrowing while interest rates are high
findings.detail: The council has maintained high levels of internal borrowing (drawing down £248m of cash reserves) to minimize external borrowing and offset rising interest rates. This is a deliberate finite-resource strategy: once cash reserves are depleted, the council will be forced to borrow externally at whatever rates prevail. The council states it is confident reserves can support high internal borrowing for 2026/27, but uncertainty exists for 2027/28 onwards.
findings.matters: The council is consuming a finite resource (accumulated cash reserves) to manage temporary interest rate conditions; if the capital programme accelerates, operational cash needs increase, or rates remain elevated longer than expected, the council could be forced to borrow externally at unfavourable rates with weakened negotiating position
findings.figures: Internal borrowing £248m; cash investment balances £16m at 31 March 2026; council confident reserves support high internal borrowing only for 2026/27
findings.quote: Furthermore, the internal borrowing level has remained high to offset the impact from increasing interest rates and volatility in the market. The Council will look to minimise new external borrowing through utilising its cash balances.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management 202526 - Outturn - draft for CLT, 25/06/2026 Executive, 07/07/2026 Executive Briefing
findings.headline: HRA external borrowing exceeded prudential indicator limit by £6m (£101m vs £95m forecast)
findings.detail: The council's Housing Revenue Account external borrowing reached £101m as of 31 March 2026, exceeding the Treasury Management Strategy estimate of £95m by approximately 6%. The council took this deliberate decision to lock in interest rates before the PWLB HRA discount expires (March 2027). While the council argues this is acceptable because external borrowing remains below the CFR (£105m), this represents a known departure from agreed prudential indicator limits.
findings.matters: Deliberate breach of prudential indicators raises questions about risk governance and whether limits are properly calibrated; a lender should understand whether the council treats agreed limits as flexible when strategic advantage exists
findings.figures: HRA external borrowing £101m vs strategy estimate £95m (£6m overage, 6%); HRA CFR £105m
findings.quote: HRA external borrowing as of 31 March 2026 was £101m, which was higher than the strategy estimate of £95m. This has been planned to secure more external borrowing for the HRA to provide more certainty of the interest rate.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management 202526 - Outturn - draft for CLT, 25/06/2026 Executive, 07/07/2026 Executive Briefing
findings.headline: Council expects to require external borrowing in 2026/27 but cannot forecast 2027/28 onwards
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it expects to need external borrowing in the current financial year (2026/27) to support the capital programme. However, the council cannot provide forward certainty beyond this point, stating 'The impacts for 2027/28 onwards are being monitored and will be considered as part of the budget setting process' in February 2027. This suggests the capital programme is not self-financing and ongoing external funding is required.
findings.matters: Ongoing external borrowing need indicates the capital programme is structurally dependent on debt financing; forward uncertainty beyond 12 months limits the council's planning visibility and a lender's ability to assess medium-term refinancing risk
findings.figures: Expected borrowing need 2026/27 (timing TBD); uncertainly extends beyond February 2027
findings.quote: It is expected that the Council may need to borrow next financial year to support the capital programme. The timing of this borrowing requirement will continue to be monitored.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management 202526 - Outturn - draft for CLT, 25/06/2026 Executive, 07/07/2026 Executive Briefing
findings.headline: The Council faces severe financial pressures from the 3-year Local Government Finance Settlement and economic shocks
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it faces severe financial pressures resulting from the 3-year LGFS and multiple economic pressures including COVID-19, Brexit, wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, rising prices, and increasing cost of debt. The council emphasizes that resources must be optimised and focused on vulnerable residents and highest priorities, suggesting difficult budget choices ahead.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the baseline financial stress driving the council's treasury decisions and risk appetite; councils under sustained financial pressure are more likely to run down reserves or take on unfavourable debt
findings.figures: No quantified figures; statement made in financial implications section
findings.quote: The Council faces severe financial pressures as a result of the 3-year Local Government Finance Settlement and a number of economic and social pressures including COVID-19, Brexit, the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and rising prices.

findings.headline: £3.51m Adult Social Care Accommodation Transformation carry forward as council struggles to identify suitable properties
findings.detail: The council budgeted £3.51m for adult social care accommodation but has carried the full amount forward. The report states the council is "proving more difficult and timelier to identify appropriate accommodation but works progressing to speed up identification and delivery which would reduce current and expected increases in revenue costs." The delayed capital investment forces services to continue being funded from revenue budgets at higher cost.
findings.matters: When capital investment is delayed, services must continue from revenue budgets at higher ongoing cost, creating unplanned revenue pressure that affects the council's underlying financial position and increases demand on constrained revenue budgets.
findings.figures: £3.510m carry forward
findings.quote: budget set to allow development of opportunities. Proving more difficult and timelier to identify appropriate accommodation but works progressing to speed up identification and delivery which would reduce current and expected increases in revenue costs.

findings.headline: £3.15m HRA borrowing for Afghan Resettlement Programme homes will be repaid solely from rental income
findings.detail: The council is borrowing via the Housing Revenue Account to acquire 6 homes for temporary accommodation. While £1.33m is secured as ringfenced grant and £630k from S106 contributions, repayment of the remaining balance is dependent on "additional HRA borrowing and repaid in full via rental income from the properties." Repayment depends entirely on achieving letting targets in the temporary and supported housing market.
findings.matters: New HRA borrowing increases total council debt; repayment is contingent on rental income in a potentially volatile supported housing market, creating revenue risk if lettings underperform.
findings.figures: £3,150,000 total budget, £1,328,500 grant, £630,000 S106, remainder HRA borrowing
findings.quote: with the remaining funding coming from additional HRA borrowing and repaid in full via rental income from the properties

findings.headline: South Wokingham Distributor Road carries forward £19.3m due to scheme complexities and funding issues
findings.detail: A major infrastructure project shows a substantial £19.305m carry forward, with the council noting the delay "reflects delays and the complexities of the wider scheme and required funding." The specific reference to "required funding" suggests unresolved or uncertain funding sources for completing the project.
findings.matters: Large infrastructure projects depend on identified funding sources such as developer contributions or borrowing. Delays and unresolved funding complexities indicate delivery risk or the need for additional council borrowing to complete.
findings.figures: £19.305m carry forward
findings.quote: South Wokingham Distributor Road – reflects delays and the complexities of the wider scheme and required funding.

findings.headline: Renewable energy invest-to-save schemes flagged for viability review after £4.2m in identified savings
findings.detail: The council has identified £4.188m in savings from renewable energy infrastructure projects while noting that "further work is necessary to ensure invest to save schemes financial viability", indicating these schemes may not deliver expected returns. Two major solar farm projects are also delayed: Solar Farm Barkham (£22.4m carry forward) and Solar Farm 2 (£11.9m carry forward), with Barkham specifically held up by grid connection issues.
findings.matters: Investment-to-save schemes are supposed to generate revenue to reduce reliance on borrowing. A viability review suggests they may fall short, affecting the council's financial sustainability and increasing future borrowing needs.
findings.figures: £4.188m savings identified, £22.395m (Solar Farm Barkham), £11.887m (Solar Farm 2)
findings.quote: Renewable Energy Infrastructure projects - saving identified as part of 26/27 MTFP planning. Further work to ensure invest to save schemes financial viability

findings.headline: Children's placements costs increasing with uncertainty about continued asylum funding
findings.detail: Children's Services overspent by £0.2m due to increased complexity and cost of child placements. Costs from asylum-seeking children are currently mitigated by specific grants, but the council has flagged uncertainty about whether these grants will continue to fully cover costs in future years.
findings.matters: Loss or reduction of specific grants would create budget pressure in a service already facing placement cost inflation
findings.figures: £0.2m overspend; Children's Services budget £53.686m
findings.quote: The costs being seen from Children Seeking Safety through Asylum continue to be mitigated by specific grants, however there is uncertainty around these continuing to fully cover cost in future.

findings.headline: General Fund balance of £10.1m provides minimal headroom above policy minimum of £9m
findings.detail: General Fund balance at 31 March 2026 is £10.1m, in line with the 5% net expenditure minimum established in reserves policy. This provides only £1.1m above the minimum threshold, constraining financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Minimal reserve buffer limits ability to absorb unexpected costs, service volatility, or economic shocks, and leaves little flexibility for strategic investments
findings.figures: General Fund balance £10.1m; policy minimum £9m (5% of £203.066m net expenditure)
findings.quote: There is no generally applicable minimum level of reserves, although, previous guidance from the Audit Commission suggested a crude measure as 5% of net expenditure (excluding the Dedicated Schools Grant) as a minimum. This equates to c£9m

findings.headline: DSG cumulative deficit of £52.9m with £17.7m in-year overspend on £224m allocation
findings.detail: Deficit driven by High Needs Block pressures from increased EHCP placements and complexity. In-year position improved by £6.8m against budget projection. Safety Valve agreement with DfE has yielded £13.2m of £20m funding. Central government committed to supporting 90% of 2025/26 deficit on approval of Local SEND Reform Plan.
findings.matters: Large structural deficit in delegated schools funding creates ongoing dependency on central government support mechanisms; any change in policy would directly impact council finances
findings.figures: £17.7m in-year deficit (7.9% of allocation); cumulative deficit £52.9m; Safety Valve funding received £13.2m of £20m committed
findings.quote: The overspend on the DSG relates to ongoing pressure in the High Needs Block, driven largely by a continued increase in the number and costs of children and young people with Education Health Care Plan's (EHCP's), with increasing complexity of need, and demand for specialist placements.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspent by £1.2m, driven by demand growth and market cost pressures
findings.detail: Overspend increased from Q3 and reflects growth in caseloads, complexity of need, and higher-cost care packages in older people's and learning disability services. Additional pressure from equipment provider failure causing transitional costs and operational disruption as new contract stabilises.
findings.matters: Growing structural demand and market-driven cost inflation in the council's largest service signals recurring budget pressure and reduced ability to achieve savings
findings.figures: £1.2m overspend; Adult Social Care budget £76.857m
findings.quote: growth and demand continuing across the service, particularly within older people's and learning disability provision. This reflects a combination of increased caseloads, the complexity of need and higher-cost packages of care, alongside ongoing market pressures affecting care costs.

findings.headline: Building Control internal audit confirmed significant risk from shortage of qualified staff.
findings.detail: Internal audit confirmed management's assessment that a shortage of qualified building control staff poses a significant risk. The council has an action plan due September 2026 to address this.
findings.matters: Building Control understaffing creates regulatory compliance and service delivery risk, and may constrain the council's ability to support local development and growth.
findings.figures: Action plan due September 2026
findings.quote: The Building Control Internal Audit confirmed management's assessment that the shortage of qualified building control staff posed a significant risk to the Council.

findings.headline: Significant capital programme carry-forwards signal governance and delivery challenges.
findings.detail: The council has identified opportunities to improve financial governance of the capital programme. Significant carry-forwards between financial years indicate either planning weaknesses or delivery delays. A detailed review of three years' spending has identified additional areas for challenge.
findings.matters: Persistent capital carry-forwards indicate the council either over-plans its capital programme or struggles to deliver it, both of which signal financial management and delivery capability issues.
findings.figures: Significant carry forwards of capital between financial years identified
findings.quote: The Council has identified opportunities to improve the financial governance of the capital programme last year. There have been significant carry forwards of capital between financial years.

findings.headline: Ofsted/CQC joint SEND inspection (January 2026) identified areas requiring improvement; ombudsman complaints in SEND above council average.
findings.detail: A joint inspection found the council has areas to improve in SEND service delivery. Eight of 13 upheld ombudsman complaints in the year related to children with SEND. The council reports 7.1 upheld complaints per 100,000 residents versus a 5.2 average elsewhere.
findings.matters: SEND service failures create regulatory intervention risk, reputational damage, and indicate gaps in governance over statutory duties. Above-average ombudsman complaints signal service delivery and governance weaknesses.
findings.figures: 8 of 13 upheld ombudsman findings related to SEND; 7.1 upheld complaints per 100k residents vs 5.2 average
findings.quote: In January 2026 Ofsted and the Care Quality Commission undertook a joint Wokingham Area SEND Inspection. There are a number of areas where the Council can improve

findings.headline: Statement of Accounts remains qualified despite improvement from prior disclaimed opinions.
findings.detail: Prior three years (2021/22 to 2023/24) received disclaimed audit opinions. The 2024/25 accounts now carry a qualified opinion, meaning auditors can assess the accounts as fairly stated but with gaps in assurance. The council is working toward an unqualified opinion for 2025/26.
findings.matters: A qualified audit opinion indicates unresolved weaknesses in financial controls or record-keeping that create audit gaps, signalling financial reporting quality below best practice.
findings.figures: 2024/25 qualified opinion; prior three years disclaimed
findings.quote: The external audit opinion for 2024/25 has moved to a qualified opinion which means "there are some gaps in assurance, but overall the accounts are fairly stated." from a disclaimer of opinion

findings.headline: Financial sustainability beyond the current three-year settlement represents a significant governance challenge for the council.
findings.detail: The council explicitly names financial sustainability as a major governance issue. It faces increasing demand for services and cost pressures with limited ability to increase income. The three-year local government financial settlement creates significant pressures outlined in detail in the Chief Financial Officer's report.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand how the council will manage an unsustainable financial position when the current three-year settlement ends, particularly given demographic and service demand pressures.
findings.figures: Three-year local government financial settlement identified as creating significant financial pressures
findings.quote: the financial sustainability of the authority beyond the existing financial settlement represents a significant challenge given increasing demand for services, cost pressures and limitations on increasing income

findings.headline: Debt trajectory assumes successful achievement of forecasted revenues and transformation savings
findings.detail: The council projects debt will rise in line with capital investment then decline as income from projects and cost savings materialise. General fund debt is forecast to rise well above £300m through the forecast period before declining. The strategy is contingent on these assumptions holding, with the council noting uncertainty pending level of further investment beyond the three-year programme.
findings.matters: If projected revenues or cost savings don't materialise as forecast, debt will continue rising rather than declining, creating refinancing pressure and potentially reducing covenant headroom for the council
findings.figures: General fund debt projected to rise above £300m, Housing Revenue Account debt to exceed £120m; repayment profile depends on income achievement
findings.quote: The Council are expecting debt to rise in line with the capital programme and then it is expected to reduce over time as income is generated from these projects and cost savings are realised, pending the level of further investment identified beyond the three year capital programme.

findings.headline: Developer contributions of £72.7m (21% of programme) dependent on continued development activity
findings.detail: Developer contributions (s106 and CIL) are forecast at £28.5m (2026/27), £26.2m (2027/28), and £18.0m (2028/29), totalling £72.7m over three years. Any slowdown in development across the borough would reduce this income stream, creating a funding gap requiring substitution from borrowing or programme reduction.
findings.matters: A significant share of capital funding depends on external factors (development activity) outside the council's control; any downturn in development could force difficult trade-offs between capital programmes
findings.figures: Developer contributions £28.5m, £26.2m, £18.0m = £72.7m total (21% of £347.3m total capital resources)
findings.quote: Like most Local Authorities, the Council has limited capital resources available, and these are allocated to each scheme to ensure best value for money by maximising the use of grants, developer funding and capital receipts

findings.headline: Majority of capital programme relies on revenues from regeneration, leisure and social care projects
findings.detail: The council explicitly funds £148.9m of borrowing through 'supported borrowing' and 'invest to save' schemes where income is forecast to exceed financing costs. These include regeneration projects, town centre property acquisition, leisure facilities, energy efficiency, and social care placements. If revenues underperform forecasts, the council has no alternative funding source.
findings.matters: A lender must understand the capital programme funding depends on achieving forecasted revenues from projects where costs are certain and revenues are forecast - material underperformance would force programme cuts or additional borrowing
findings.figures: Supported borrowing £148.9m, General fund borrowing £16.3m, total borrowing £165.2m out of £347.3m programme
findings.quote: A significant part of the Council's capital programme is either self-financing or makes a surplus where the income generated is greater than the cost of financing and therefore is available to fund other council services.

findings.headline: Borrowing costs remain high and are projected to stay elevated despite easing inflation, increasing council's capital financing burden.
findings.detail: Interest rates have remained elevated and the council expects them to remain so even as inflation moderates. This increases the ongoing cost of financing the capital programme (roads, schools, housing). The CIPFA resilience index flags that interest payable as a percentage of net revenue expenditure is a 'relatively higher risk position' for Wokingham.
findings.matters: Capital financing costs are fixed once incurred. Rising rates make every new borrowing decision more expensive in perpetuity. This constrains the council's ability to fund the capital strategy without additional revenue cuts.
findings.figures: Council holds gross external debt at the lower risk end for unitary authorities; interest payable flagged as 'relatively higher risk'; exact borrowing levels and rates not specified.
findings.quote: The cost of borrowing has remained high and is projected to continue at these levels even when inflationary pressures eased.

findings.headline: Population growing at 15% since 2011 (23,000 residents), with increasing migration and an ageing population structure, straining services without corresponding funding growth.
findings.detail: Wokingham has added 23,000 residents over the past decade. This growth is forecast to continue, with a high proportion of inward migration and a growing elderly population. These structural shifts require investment in social care, housing, and transport—exactly the services now facing funding cuts.
findings.matters: Demographic tailwinds require investment to manage safely. Instead, the council faces funding headwinds. This mismatch creates execution risk and potential service degradation.
findings.figures: 23,000 residents added 2011–2021; 15% growth; ongoing growth forecast; growing proportion of elderly population and inward migration.
findings.quote: growing local population (15% increase or 23000 residents from 2011 to 2021) which will continue into future years and with it the added complexity and diversity of a high proportion of inward migration and an increasingly elderly population.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care demand rising in numbers and complexity amid a deteriorating care provider market; charging reform postponed.
findings.detail: Demand for Adult Social Care is rising in both volume and complexity. The National Living Wage increases and National Insurance rises are squeezing care provider margins, risking market exit and reduced placement capacity. The Government's postponed charging reform leaves the council exposed to further pressure once reforms land.
findings.matters: A tightening care market coupled with rising demand creates a dual risk: unmet need (reputational/safeguarding) or emergency placements at inflated cost. The council has low social care cost ratios currently (CIPFA index) but this trend will erode that position.
findings.figures: Already the lowest social care cost ratio vs other councils; National Living Wage rises and NI increases cited as imminent pressures.
findings.quote: Already demand in this area is increasing both in terms of numbers and complexity, which will be exacerbated through further pressures on both the care market and the health system. The recent further enhancement to the National living wage and the previous increase in National Insurance contributions will put further stress on an already struggling care market.

findings.headline: £54m DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) deficit forecast to 31 March 2026, though Government has committed to funding 90% of this amount.
findings.detail: The accumulated High Needs deficit is estimated at £54m as of end-March 2026. However, the recent Government announcement that it will fund 90% of deficits accruing to 31 March 2026, plus continuation of the Statutory Override to March 2028, significantly reduces council liability. The residual debt and interest costs are still being quantified.
findings.matters: This was a catastrophic liability (£54m) but government intervention has reduced it. However, deficits arising between April 2026 and March 2028 will only receive 'appropriate' (undefined) funding, leaving a material gap unfunded.
findings.figures: £54m accumulated deficit as of 31 March 2026; Government funding 90% of this; residual debt liability and interest cost to be determined.
findings.quote: Council are now estimating a deficit reserve at 31st March 2026 of c£54m in this area (inclusive of Safety Valve payments and use of the Equalisation Fund). The Government has announced that it will fund 90% of deficits accruing to 31st March 2026.

findings.headline: Wokingham receives the lowest core government funding per head of any unitary authority in England—£158 per head, versus £1,050 for Blackpool.
findings.detail: Even accounting for deprivation indices, Wokingham is systematically underfunded. The gap to average unitary authority funding is £76m–£96m per annum, and Wokingham would receive £172m additional per annum if funded at Blackpool's level. This is a structural funding disadvantage in the formula, not a temporary shortfall.
findings.matters: This is not just a current settlement problem; it reflects a systemic bias in the funding formula that is unlikely to be corrected. Wokingham cannot out-save its way out of this.
findings.figures: £158 per head (Wokingham 2026/27) vs £1,050 (Blackpool); £76m–£96m annual shortfall vs unitary average; would receive £172m additional if funded like Blackpool.
findings.quote: Wokingham has the lowest levels of core Government funding in England... Blackpool has the highest score on the Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) and receives six times the funding per head that Wokingham receives (£158 compared to £1,050 per head).

findings.headline: CFO warns the council may need Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) in 2028/29 if the funding gap and DSG recovery are not resolved.
findings.detail: The CFO's conclusion is conditional but clear: the structural funding deficit, combined with uncertainty over the DSG recovery settlement and the council's ability to deliver planned savings, creates a material risk that Exceptional Financial Support will be needed by year 3.
findings.matters: EFS is a last resort—it signals a council in serious structural distress. The fact that the CFO is flagging this risk suggests lenders should model for liquidity strain in 2028/29 and question the achievability of the savings plan.
findings.figures: 2028/29 is identified as the year of greatest risk; DSG deficit alone could add £54m liability if not government-funded.
findings.quote: Depending on the Government's DSG repayment requirements and the Council ability to deliver on existing savings/efficiencies as well as identifying considerably more, the Council may need to consider the need for Exceptional Financial Support in this year.

findings.headline: 2026/27 budget is balanced only through drawing down reserves over three years—a finite solution.
findings.detail: The council cannot balance 2026/27 through services cuts or council tax alone. It is instead drawing 'a sizeable contribution from Reserves' to plug the gap. This is a three-year drawdown, not a one-off hit, meaning reserves are being consumed systematically.
findings.matters: Reserves are ammunition for crises. Using them to balance routine budget shortfalls accelerates the date when the council runs out of contingency. By 2028/29, reserves will be depleted and no further drawdown is possible.
findings.figures: General Fund balance forecast shows drawdown from ~£53m (actual 2025) through 2026–2028; council tax is being increased to the maximum allowed (5%) to slow the burn.
findings.quote: The budget proposals balance the General Fund budget for 2026/27, although this does require a sizeable contribution from Reserves that will be drawn down over a three-year period to ensure the use of Reserves does not create an additional budget pressure within this three-year period.

findings.headline: Council is currently overspending by £1.3m in 2025/26 and actively working to eliminate it before next year.
findings.detail: The Q3 revenue monitoring report flagged a £1.3m in-year overspend. The document notes 'work continues in 2025/26 to reduce the in-year overspend', suggesting active remediation but no closure yet.
findings.matters: Current budget discipline is already strained before the 2026/27 cuts land. An in-year shortfall plus a multiyear funding cliff suggests execution risk on the savings plan.
findings.figures: £1.3m overspend in 2025/26 (Q3 monitoring).
findings.quote: work continues in 2025/26 to reduce the in-year overspend of c£1.3m, as reported in the quarter three revenue monitoring, to restore reserves to higher levels.

findings.headline: Gorse Ride redevelopment is the primary driver of rising prudential borrowing
findings.detail: The council is undertaking a major HRA capital scheme, Gorse Ride Redevelopment, which will deliver affordable housing but is driving the increase in HRA debt. The scheme is expected to generate capital receipts and rental income once complete, which will fund future debt repayment.
findings.matters: The scheme is a bet on future income to service debt. If rental income growth falls short or the project overruns, the HRA's financial position deteriorates.
findings.figures: HRA capital programme 2026/27: £27.7m total, with £8.4m supported borrowing. Total HRA capital programme: £74.0m over three years.
findings.quote: A key driver for the increase in the prudential borrowing relates to Gorse Ride Redevelopment. Capital receipts and additional rental income will be received once the project is completed and will be used as future VRP to reduce the HRA CFR balance.

findings.headline: PWLB HRA discount expires March 2026 and refinancing approach changes with interest rate expectations
findings.detail: The council has been using a short-term borrowing strategy for HRA debt while interest rates remain high, betting on future rate decreases. The government discount on PWLB borrowing for HRA expires at end of March 2026. This timing matters for refinancing decisions on legacy loans.
findings.matters: If interest rates don't fall as expected, the council could lock in higher costs. The discount expiry removes a financial relief at a moment of HRA strain.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this extract; relates to legacy PWLB loans from 2012 Housing Revenue Account self-financing
findings.quote: The government has introduced an additional discount on PWLB borrowing for the HRA, this is due to expire in March 2026 and will be monitored closely as part of any borrowing decisions.

findings.headline: HRA debt repayment frozen: VRP payments falling due to revenue pressures and high interest rates
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account has stopped meaningful debt repayment. VRP (voluntary revenue provision) payments are described as 'lower than previous years' due to 'increased pressures on the revenue budget, lower levels of rent increases and interest rates remaining higher than expected'. The council notes this requires close monitoring to ensure HRA financial stability.
findings.matters: Frozen debt repayment means HRA debt will keep growing. Combined with rising interest rates, this squeezes the HRA budget and threatens rent affordability and service delivery.
findings.figures: HRA CFR: £106m (2025/26) → £109m (2026/27) → £119m (2027/28) → £124m (2028/29); Ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream HRA: 20.11% rising to 22.52%
findings.quote: due to increased pressures on the revenue budget, lower levels of rent increases and interest rates remaining higher than expected, VRP payments are estimated to be lower than previous years over the medium term financial plan

findings.headline: Gross external borrowing rising sharply from £140m to £240m in General Fund
findings.detail: General Fund external debt will jump 71% in 2026/27 as the council funds major capital projects. While debt is expected to stabilise after that, the immediate jump is substantial and will increase annual interest costs.
findings.matters: Lenders need to see the council can service this level of debt. The jump reflects capital ambition but also increases financial risk if revenues fall or interest rates remain elevated.
findings.figures: Gross external borrowing – General Fund: £140m (2025/26 forecast) → £240m (2026/27) → £247m (2027/28) → £246m (2028/29)
findings.quote: Gross external borrowing – General Fund (GF) £140m £240m £247m £246m

findings.headline: DSG deficit eroding internal borrowing capacity and forcing external borrowing
findings.detail: The council has historically minimised external borrowing by using cash balances and reserves (internal borrowing). But DSG deficit pressures mean this will become increasingly difficult. The council cannot charge DSG interest costs to the ringfenced schools account, creating an additional burden that will worsen interest costs on external debt if government does not resolve the issue.
findings.matters: Rising external borrowing needs and interest costs reduce cash available for services. This is a structural squeeze rather than a temporary budget gap.
findings.figures: Ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream GF (excl. DSG): 1.10% (2026/27) rising to 1.48% (2027/28); with DSG included: 2.62% rising to 3.36%
findings.quote: Over the next three, the Councils ability to hold higher levels of internal borrowing will become more difficult if the Government do not address the significant financial burden from the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit. If the deficit continues as projected without government intervention, the Council will have less cash balances and will be required to borrow more externally.

findings.headline: Waste mobilisation faces Emissions Trading Scheme cost increases
findings.detail: Wokingham is mobilising a new waste collection and street cleansing contract (June 2026) and re-procuring Re3 contract (target 2031). Identified risk includes 'Emissions Trading Scheme additional costs due to rule changes.' Impact magnitude unquantified but flagged as a discrete risk factor.
findings.matters: ETS costs are non-discretionary operational expenses that will compress waste and environmental budgets unless absorbed by service cuts or efficiency gains.
findings.figures: Mobilisation June 2026; ETS impact unquantified
findings.quote: Emissions Trading Scheme additional costs due to rule changes

findings.headline: Adult social care provider market unstable; failures in past 12 months
findings.detail: Wokingham reports that 'there have been provider failures within the last year' in adult social care. The council identifies risk of carrying 'more statutory risk and higher waiting lists, or that we are unable to source care that is good quality and suitable for a vulnerable resident.' Capacity pressures remain classified as 'very high' risk.
findings.matters: Provider failures create care capacity gaps forcing councils to commission emergency placements at premium rates or delay care provision, destabilising adult social care budgets.
findings.figures: At least one provider failure in past 12 months
findings.quote: There have been provider failures within the last year

findings.headline: Housing regulatory inspection carries unquantified financial impact risk
findings.detail: New regulation under the Social Housing Regulation Bill 2024 introduces building compliance and tenant safety requirements. Wokingham has completed mock inspection (June 2025) and identified the risk that 'any regulatory inspection could have a significant potential impact on finances within the HRA and across the whole Council.' Impact scope is unquantified.
findings.matters: Regulatory inspection outcomes regularly trigger substantial capital investment requirements for stock remediation and can destabilise HRA financial projections.
findings.figures: Impact scope: HRA and council-wide (unquantified)
findings.quote: The outcome of any regulatory inspection could have a significant potential impact on finances within the HRA and across the whole Council

findings.headline: Asylum accommodation costs being funded from council reserves
findings.detail: Wokingham has statutory duty to support children in care, including 42 children under the National Transfer Scheme for children seeking asylum. Government grant funding does not cover actual placement and accommodation costs. The council is explicitly using its 'refigure/migration reserve' to offset these costs—funding recurring statutory service costs from one-off reserves rather than ongoing budget.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion for recurring statutory service costs signals structural budget deficit; this pattern accelerates reserve exhaustion and creates future budget crisis.
findings.figures: Minimum 42 children mandated by National Transfer Scheme; costs offset by reserve drawdown
findings.quote: Cost currently being offset by use of the council refigure/migration reserve

findings.headline: Adult Social Care Fair Pay Agreement (2028) will trigger major cost shock
findings.detail: The council's risk assessment flags Adult Social Care as 'very high' risk and explicitly notes that the government's announced Adult Social Care Fair Pay Agreement, expected 2028, will compound existing pressures. This will materially increase wage and cost pressures on an already-strained social care sector.
findings.matters: This is a confirmed, forward-dated cost increase that councils cannot avoid or mitigate; it affects both commissioning costs and in-house service budgets.
findings.figures: Fair Pay Agreement implementation 2028
findings.quote: This risk remains very high compounded by the recent announcement of the Adult Social Care Fair Pay Agreement (expected 2028)

findings.headline: High Needs Block overspend risk of £10m+ with no mitigation path
findings.detail: Wokingham identifies escalating costs for children with SEND as high-risk due to increasing need and complexity. The register notes this risk is 'expected that the risk will never be fully mitigated unless the funding position changes drastically with heavy investment in this area.' Special Free Schools funding and delivery are delayed (target dates now 2028-2030).
findings.matters: SEND overspends are a systemic pressure across English councils and this represents high-confidence future costs that depress financial resilience without new government funding.
findings.figures: £10m+ overspend risk identified
findings.quote: there is a risk of overspend on the High Needs Block (£10m+), risking a substantial impact on the Council's finances

findings.headline: Risk of Section 114 notice if budget resilience measures fail
findings.detail: Wokingham faces significant cost pressures from inflation, national minimum wage increases, loss of income, higher borrowing costs, and demand from cost-of-living effects. The risk register explicitly identifies that if these pressures are not managed, the council risks reserve depletion, service cuts, failure to meet statutory duties, and ultimately a Section 114 notice (formal insolvency declaration).
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice signals severe financial distress and triggers government intervention; it constrains borrowing and service delivery capacity fundamentally.
findings.figures: Potential High Needs Block overspend £10m+
findings.quote: if unchecked a Section 114 notice

findings.headline: Year-end borrowings increased by £12.3 million to £200.1 million, increasing debt burden whilst addressing structural deficit.
findings.detail: Gross borrowing increased from £187.9m to £200.1m. Against a background of structural revenue deficits and reserve drawdowns, the increase in borrowings signals the council is simultaneously managing liquidity whilst eroding asset position, a combination that reduces financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Growing borrowings combined with structural deficits and reserve depletion creates a tightening financial position. The council has less capacity to absorb additional shocks or invest in transformation needed to meet the £20m savings target.
findings.figures: Year-end borrowings 2024/25: £200,145k; 2023/24: £187,889k (increase of £12,256k)
findings.quote: Year-end borrowings 200,145

findings.headline: Adult Social Care structural overspends continuing: £281k overspend in 2024/25, £391k overspend in Q2 2025/26, driven by increased cost and scarcity of placements.
findings.detail: Adult Social Care overspent by £281k in the completed year due to increased cost and scarcity of placements. This has continued into 2025/26 with Q2 monitoring showing £391k overspend in ASC alone (out of a total projected £1m overspend). This appears to be a structural demand and pricing issue rather than a one-off variance.
findings.matters: Persistent overspends in social care suggest the council's budget assumptions do not reflect the market reality of placement costs and demand growth. This is a leading indicator of budget sustainability risk given social care is typically the largest and most volatile spend area in council budgets.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care overspend 2024/25: £281k; Q2 2025/26 overspend £391k
findings.quote: This is mainly due to increased cost and scarcity of placements, which is not unique to the Council.

findings.headline: General Fund balance improvement masked by planned £9 million reserve drawdown; actual revenue result was £251k overspend.
findings.detail: The General Fund balance increased from £9.5m to £11.1m, but this improvement required a planned £9m drawdown from earmarked reserves. The underlying revenue position for the year was a £251k overspend. This indicates the council is running a structural deficit that is being bridged by reserves rather than achieving operational balance.
findings.matters: A council that depends on reserve drawdowns to maintain a positive General Fund is not operationally sustainable. Each year of structural deficit erodes the reserve buffer available to absorb future shocks, particularly important given the DSG deficit cliff in 2028.
findings.figures: General Fund balance £11.1m (2024/25) vs £9.5m (2023/24); revenue outturn £251k overspend; planned earmarked reserves drawdown £9m
findings.quote: The General Fund balance remains relatively healthy with £11.1 million at the end of 24/25 (£9.5 million in 23/24), albeit with planned reserves drawdown of £9 million to achieve this.

findings.headline: Savings plan underperforming: achieved £7.8m of £11.6m planned savings target (31% shortfall), whilst council requires £20m savings over next three years.
findings.detail: The council set ambitious savings targets of £11.6m for 2024/25 but the Savings Monitoring Report shows only £7.8m were achieved. Meanwhile, the council acknowledges that up to £20m of savings will be needed over the next three years to maintain the current financial position. This execution gap is significant given the scale of future savings required.
findings.matters: Persistent shortfalls on savings targets create material risk that the council cannot deliver its Medium Term Financial Plan. If the council continues to miss savings by 30% on £20m targets, it would face a £6m+ shortfall annually, making the financial position unsustainable without further reserve draws or borrowing.
findings.figures: £11.6 million planned savings 2024/25; £7.8 million achieved; £20 million savings needed over next 3 years
findings.quote: The Council expected to achieve £9.4 million of these in the MTFP Savings Tracker as at February 2025 reviewed. The Savings Monitoring Report at year end suggests £7.8 million were achieved.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £36.9 million explicitly flagged as major concern, with statutory override expiring March 2028.
findings.detail: The DSG deficit has doubled in one year from £20.2m to £36.9m. The council acknowledges this as a major concern and has a recovery plan plus involvement in the Safety Valve scheme. The accounting override allowing councils to exclude this from their main budget expires 31 March 2028; if the override is removed or reformed without progress, the council would face significant financial instability and the deficit would consolidate into the General Fund balance.
findings.matters: A £36.9m deficit represents 330% of the General Fund balance and creates cliff risk when the statutory protection expires. Wokingham would become technically insolvent if the override ended without substantial progress, making this a material going-concern consideration for lenders.
findings.figures: £36.9 million DSG deficit at 31 March 2025 (£20.2 million in 2023/24); statutory override expires 31 March 2028
findings.quote: Wokingham recognise their £36.9 million deficit is a major concern and have outlined a DSG Deficit Recovery Plan, as well as being involved in the Safety Valve Programme with the Department for Education.

news_drafts.headline: Multiple major capital schemes show deferrals of 50% or more, including Toutley depot (56%), ASC accommodation transformation (73%), and MEES investment (52%)
news_drafts.lead: Multiple major capital schemes being deferred at rates above 50% suggests potential systemic constraints in capital delivery, whether in planning, procurement, funding, or execution across multiple service areas

news_drafts.headline: Grays Farm sports hub has £5.3 million (84%) of its £6.3 million current-year budget deferred, the most heavily slipped project
news_drafts.lead: Significant deferral of a major service infrastructure project suggests material delays in design, procurement, or planning that warrant investigation and may impact when intended service benefits are realised

news_drafts.headline: £19.2 million (36.5% of the current-year £52.7 million approved capital budget) is being carried forward to future years
news_drafts.lead: Material mid-year capital programme slippage of over one-third of approved spend affects future budget pressures and raises questions about the council's ability to deliver capital projects within planned timescales
